fp2_complex_powers.description: Use and prove de Moivre’s theorem, handle negative powers and find all branches of rational powers.

sections.title: How does multiplication move an Argand point?
sections.label: Rotate and scale
sections.intro: Write each non-zero number as a modulus times a unit rotation.

blocks.html: Multiplication multiplies the moduli and adds the arguments. Division divides the moduli and subtracts the arguments.

figure.alt: Multiplication by a complex number scales one vector and rotates it.
figure.caption: Multiplication by \(2\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\frac{\pi}{3}}\) doubles the length and turns the vector through \(\tfrac{\pi}{3}\) anticlockwise.

blocks.html: An argument sum may lie outside the principal interval. Add or subtract a full turn to bring it back.

blocks.title: Multiply through the principal interval
blocks.prompt:
Let \(z=4\,\mathrm e^{\frac{5 i \pi}{6}}\) and \(w=2\,\mathrm e^{\frac{3 i \pi}{4}}\).

Give the modulus and the coefficient of \(\pi\) in the principal argument of \(zw\).
blocks.hint: Combine arguments first, then bring the result into the principal interval.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the moduli and add the arguments.

\(zw=8\,\mathrm e^{- \frac{5 i \pi}{12}}\), with the argument in \((-\pi,\pi]\).

blocks.html: Start by writing the requested interval.

sections.title: How can I prove the positive integer formula?
sections.label: Proof
sections.intro: Use the trigonometric angle-addition formulae in the induction step.

blocks.html: Assume the result for \(n=k\), then multiply by \(\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta\) to obtain the result at \(k+1\).
Check \(n=1\) before stating the induction conclusion.

blocks.title: Identify the base case
blocks.prompt:
The induction proves the formula for positive integer powers.

Which check provides the base case?
blocks.hint: The first positive integer is 1. An induction base case starts the stated range.
blocks.solution: At \(n=1\) this is exactly the definition of \(u\). The induction step then passes from \(k\) to \(k+1\).

blocks.html: For modulus \(r\) factor out \(r^n\) separately.

sections.title: What changes for a negative exponent?
sections.label: Reciprocal
sections.intro: A reciprocal reverses an argument and replaces the modulus by its reciprocal.

blocks.html: \((r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta})^{-k}=r^{-k}\mathrm e^{-\mathrm ik\theta}\) for \(r>0\).
Multiplying an angle by a negative number reverses its sense. A negative exponent is undefined at zero.

blocks.title: Use reciprocal magnitude and principal angle
blocks.prompt:
Let \(z=2\,\mathrm e^{\frac{i \pi}{4}}\).

Give the exact modulus and the coefficient of \(\pi\) in the principal argument.
blocks.hint: A negative exponent first requires a reciprocal, which reverses the argument.
blocks.solution:
Raise the modulus to the same power and multiply the argument by the exponent.

\(|z^{-5}|=\frac{1}{32},\quad \arg(z^{-5})\equiv - \frac{5 \pi}{4}\pmod{2\pi}\).

The principal argument is \(\frac{3 \pi}{4}\), so the number is \(\frac{\sqrt{2} \left(-1 + i\right)}{64}\).

blocks.html: Check the sign of the resulting imaginary component against its quadrant.

sections.title: How do I find every branch of a rational exponent?
sections.label: Rational powers
sections.intro: Write every input argument as one angle plus an integer number of full turns.

blocks.html: \((r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta})^{\frac pq}=r^{\frac pq}\exp\left(\frac{\mathrm ip}{q}(\theta+2k\pi)\right)\) for a reduced fraction \(\tfrac pq\) with \(q>0\) and \(r>0\).
Using only the principal input argument usually loses valid values.

blocks.title: Keep all branches in the positive argument interval
blocks.prompt:
Let \(z=64\,\mathrm e^{\frac{2 i \pi}{3}}\). Find all values of \(z^{\frac{2}{3}}\).

Give the complete set of coefficients of \(\pi\) in \([0,2\pi)\).

fields.label: Coefficients of π, separated by commas

blocks.hint: Use all input arguments before multiplying by the rational exponent. Do not stop after the principal input angle.
blocks.solution:
Write the input arguments as \(\frac{2 \pi}{3}+2k\pi\). Multiply each by the rational power.

Use \(k=0,\ldots,2\) and put the angles in the requested interval.

Common modulusArgument in the given interval
\(16\)\(\frac{4 \pi}{9}\)
\(16\)\(\frac{10 \pi}{9}\)
\(16\)\(\frac{16 \pi}{9}\)

There are \(3\) distinct branches. Raising any value to \(3\) gives \(z^{2}\).

blocks.html: For a reduced exponent use \(k=0,\ldots,q-1\).

sections.title: Where do the branches sit on the diagram?
sections.label: Root circle
sections.intro: Each branch has the same modulus. The full set is equally spaced around the origin.

blocks.html: The angular spacing in increasing counter-clockwise order is \(\tfrac{2\pi}{q}\). Taking successive \(k\) may skip intermediate points.
Changing the interval representation of an argument does not move its point.

blocks.title: Find the exact radius and spacing of fifth-root branches
blocks.prompt:
Let \(z=32\,\mathrm e^{\frac{i \pi}{6}}\). Find all values of \(z^{\frac{1}{5}}\).

Give the common modulus and the counter-clockwise spacing as a coefficient of \(\pi\).

blocks.hint: Use all input arguments before multiplying by the rational exponent. Do not stop after the principal input angle.
blocks.solution:
Write the input arguments as \(\frac{\pi}{6}+2k\pi\). Multiply each by the rational power.

Use \(k=0,\ldots,4\) and put the angles in the requested interval.

\(2\)\(\frac{5 \pi}{6}\)

blocks.html: Sort the final arguments in the requested interval.

sections.title: How do I check a negative rational power?
sections.label: Negative branches
sections.intro: Take a nonzero input and work with a positive modulus. A negative numerator gives the reciprocal modulus for the same positive exponent.

blocks.html: For each candidate \(w\) check \(w^q=z^p\) and confirm that the distinct branch count is \(q\).
Do not retain zero when using a negative power.

blocks.title: Find the full negative rational branch set
blocks.prompt:
Let \(z=125\,\mathrm e^{\frac{i \pi}{2}}\). Find all values of \(z^{\frac{-2}{3}}\).

Give the common modulus. Give the complete set of coefficients of \(\pi\) in \((-\pi,\pi]\).

fields.label: Coefficients of π, separated by commas

blocks.hint: Use all input arguments before multiplying by the rational exponent. Do not stop after the principal input angle.
blocks.solution:
Write the input arguments as \(\frac{\pi}{2}+2k\pi\). Multiply each by the rational power.

Use \(k=0,\ldots,2\) and put the angles in the requested interval.

Common modulusPrincipal argument
\(\frac{1}{25}\)\(- \frac{\pi}{3}\)
\(\frac{1}{25}\)\(\frac{\pi}{3}\)
\(\frac{1}{25}\)\(\pi\)

There are \(3\) distinct branches. Raising any value to \(3\) gives \(z^{-2}\).

blocks.html: When a principal value alone is requested, read the question’s convention for which branch to report.

examples.title: Combine two rotations
examples.question:
Let \(z=2\,\mathrm e^{\frac{i \pi}{3}}\) and \(w=3\,\mathrm e^{\frac{i \pi}{4}}\).

Give the modulus and the coefficient of \(\pi\) in the principal argument of \(zw\).
solution: Multiply the moduli and add the arguments.
\(zw=6\,\mathrm e^{\frac{7 i \pi}{12}}\), with the argument in \((-\pi,\pi]\).

examples.title: Undo part of a rotation by dividing
examples.question:
Let \(z=6\,\mathrm e^{- \frac{2 i \pi}{3}}\) and \(w=2\,\mathrm e^{\frac{3 i \pi}{4}}\).

Give the modulus and the coefficient of \(\pi\) in the principal argument of \(\tfrac zw\).
solution: Divide the moduli and subtract the arguments.
\(\tfrac zw=3\,\mathrm e^{\frac{7 i \pi}{12}}\), with the argument in \((-\pi,\pi]\).

examples.title: Find the induction move
examples.question:
Let \(u=\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta\). Suppose \(u^k=\cos(k\theta)+\mathrm i\sin(k\theta)\).

Which operation gives the induction step?
solution: The case \(k=1\) is immediate. Multiply the case \(k\) by \(u\) to get \(u^{k+1}\).
The real part becomes \(\cos(k\theta)\cos\theta-\sin(k\theta)\sin\theta\) and the imaginary coefficient becomes \(\sin(k\theta)\cos\theta+\cos(k\theta)\sin\theta\).
These equal \(\cos((k+1)\theta)\) and \(\sin((k+1)\theta)\). The induction proves the result for positive integers.

examples.title: Use a negative integer power
examples.question:
Let \(z=2\,\mathrm e^{\frac{i \pi}{6}}\).

Find the real and imaginary parts of \(z^{-4}\).
solution:
Raise the modulus to the same power and multiply the argument by the exponent.

\(|z^{-4}|=\frac{1}{16},\quad \arg(z^{-4})\equiv - \frac{2 \pi}{3}\pmod{2\pi}\).
The principal argument is \(- \frac{2 \pi}{3}\), so the number is \(- \frac{1}{32} - \frac{\sqrt{3} i}{32}\).

examples.title: List all cube roots of a rotated point
examples.question:
Let \(z=27\,\mathrm e^{\frac{i \pi}{2}}\). Find all values of \(z^{\frac{1}{3}}\).

Give the complete set of coefficients of \(\pi\) in \((-\pi,\pi]\).
solution:
Write the input arguments as \(\frac{\pi}{2}+2k\pi\). Multiply each by the rational power.

Use \(k=0,\ldots,2\) and put the angles in the requested interval.

Common modulusPrincipal argument
\(3\)\(- \frac{\pi}{2}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{\pi}{6}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{5 \pi}{6}\)
There are \(3\) distinct branches. Raising any value to \(3\) gives \(z^{1}\).

examples.question:
Let \(z=81\,\mathrm e^{i \pi}\). Find all values of \(z^{\frac{1}{4}}\).

Give the common modulus and the counter-clockwise spacing as a coefficient of \(\pi\).

Use \(k=0,\ldots,3\) and put the angles in the requested interval.

\(3\)\(- \frac{\pi}{4}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{\pi}{4}\)
\(3\)\(\frac{3 \pi}{4}\)
There are \(4\) distinct branches. Raising any value to \(4\) gives \(z^{1}\).

examples.question:
Let \(z=16\,\mathrm e^{\frac{i \pi}{2}}\). Find all values of \(z^{\frac{-3}{4}}\).

Give the common modulus. Give the complete set of coefficients of \(\pi\) in \((-\pi,\pi]\).

extraPractice.title: Compute two Cartesian parts using a fourth power
extraPractice.prompt:
Let \(z=3\,\mathrm e^{- \frac{i \pi}{3}}\).

Find the real and imaginary parts of \(z^{4}\).
extraPractice.hint: A negative exponent first requires a reciprocal, which reverses the argument.
extraPractice.solution:
Raise the modulus to the same power and multiply the argument by the exponent.

\(|z^{4}|=81,\quad \arg(z^{4})\equiv - \frac{4 \pi}{3}\pmod{2\pi}\).

The principal argument is \(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\), so the number is \(- \frac{81}{2} + \frac{81 \sqrt{3} i}{2}\).

extraPractice.title: Give the principal argument on the negative real axis

\(|z^{2}|=4,\quad \arg(z^{2})\equiv \pi\pmod{2\pi}\).

The principal argument is \(\pi\), so the number is \(-4\).

revision.body:
Methods to remember

Write the representation that makes the next step straightforward.

MethodWorking

Integer powers\(r^n\mathrm e^{\mathrm in\theta}\)
Rational powersUse \(\theta+2k\pi\) first.

revision.checks:
• State the chosen argument interval where needed.
  • Keep all values exactly when you can.

fp2_complex_angles.description: Derive multiple-angle identities using de Moivre’s theorem and use them to find exact roots of trigonometric polynomials.

sections.title: Why does the real part give cosine?
sections.label: Real part
sections.intro: Expanding the integer power gives a real part from even powers of \(\mathrm i\).

blocks.html: \(\cos(n\theta)=\mathrm{Re}\bigl((\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^n\bigr)\).
Even imaginary powers alternate in sign. Use \(\mathrm i^2=-1\) before collecting terms.

blocks.title: Write cosine of five times the angle as a polynomial
blocks.prompt: Let \(u=\cos\theta\). Express \(\cos(5\theta)\) as a polynomial in \(u\).
blocks.hint: Separate the real and imaginary powers of i before replacing a square.
blocks.solution:
Take the real part of \((\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^5\).

With \(a=\cos\theta,\ b=\sin\theta\), the expansion gives \(a \left(a^{4} - 10 a^{2} b^{2} + 5 b^{4}\right)\).

Use \(a^2+b^2=1\) to retain just the requested variable.

\[\cos(5\theta)=16 u^{5} - 20 u^{3} + 5 u\]

blocks.html: After expanding, use \(\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta\) when you want a polynomial in cosine.

sections.title: What does the imaginary part give?
sections.label: Imaginary part
sections.intro: Odd powers of \(\mathrm i\) give the imaginary component.

blocks.html: \(\sin(n\theta)=\mathrm{Im}\bigl((\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^n\bigr)\).
The imaginary part is the coefficient of \(\mathrm i\). It is a real number.

blocks.title: Extract the imaginary coefficients from a fifth power
blocks.prompt: Let \(u=\sin\theta\). Express \(\sin(5\theta)\) as a polynomial in \(u\).
blocks.hint: Separate the real and imaginary powers of i before replacing a square.
blocks.solution:
Take the imaginary part of \((\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^5\).

With \(a=\cos\theta,\ b=\sin\theta\), the expansion gives \(b \left(5 a^{4} - 10 a^{2} b^{2} + b^{4}\right)\).

Use \(a^2+b^2=1\) to retain just the requested variable.

\[\sin(5\theta)=16 u^{5} - 20 u^{3} + 5 u\]

blocks.html: For odd \(n\) you can replace all remaining even powers of cosine in terms of sine.

sections.title: How can I get a tangent formula?
sections.label: Tangent
sections.intro: Take sine over cosine and divide both top and bottom by the correct power of the fundamental cosine.

blocks.html: Set \(t=\tan\theta\) and use the imaginary and real components of \((1+\mathrm it)^n\).
The common domain excludes angles with \(\cos\theta=0\) or \(\cos(n\theta)=0\).

blocks.title: Find a rational expression for the tangent of a quadruple angle
blocks.prompt: Let \(t=\tan\theta\). Express \(\tan 4\theta\) as a rational expression in \(t\) on the common domain. Enter the numerator and denominator separately, using a denominator with constant term 1.
blocks.hint: Divide both parts of \(\tfrac{\sin(n\theta)}{\cos(n\theta)}\) by \(\cos^4\theta\) on the common domain.
blocks.solution:
Expand \((1+\mathrm i t)^4\) and separate its real and imaginary parts.

\(\mathrm{Re}=t^{4} - 6 t^{2} + 1,\quad \mathrm{Im}=- 4 t^{3} + 4 t\).

\[\tan 4\theta=\frac{- 4 t^{3} + 4 t}{t^{4} - 6 t^{2} + 1}\]

Require \(\cos\theta\ne0\) and \(\cos 4\theta\ne0\).

blocks.html: Keep the entire numerator and denominator when entering your answer.

sections.title: Which substitution turns the equation into a familiar angle?
sections.label: Identify the pattern
sections.intro: Recognise the polynomial as a multiple-angle expression. For cosine the range from \(0\) to \(\pi\) covers every possible input once.

blocks.html: If \(T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta)\), solve the angular equation and convert every valid angle to \(u=\cos\theta\).
One trigonometric solution family can have several angles in the permitted fundamental interval.

blocks.title: Use cosine to solve a fifth-degree equation
blocks.prompt:
Solve \(16 u^{5} - 20 u^{3} + 5 u=0\).

Give the complete set of coefficients of \(\pi\) for the corresponding angles. Use \([0,\pi]\) for cosine.
blocks.hint: Recognise the multiple-angle polynomial, then choose angles so that the real roots are listed once.
blocks.solution:
Use \(u=\cos\theta\). The polynomial was obtained from \(\cos(5\theta)-0\).

Use \(0\le\theta\le\pi\).

AnglePolynomial root
\(\frac{\pi}{10}\)\(\frac{\sqrt{2 \sqrt{5} + 10}}{4}\)
\(\frac{3 \pi}{10}\)\(\frac{\sqrt{10 - 2 \sqrt{5}}}{4}\)
\(\frac{\pi}{2}\)\(0\)
\(\frac{7 \pi}{10}\)\(- \frac{\sqrt{10 - 2 \sqrt{5}}}{4}\)
\(\frac{9 \pi}{10}\)\(- \frac{\sqrt{2 \sqrt{5} + 10}}{4}\)

These values give all distinct real roots. Repeated algebraic roots give a single value in the answer set.

blocks.html: Use exact values and keep a clear list of angles.

sections.title: How do endpoints and repeated roots affect the answer?
sections.label: Complete the set
sections.intro: Include endpoints that satisfy the original equation. Arguments in different angular families may represent one polynomial root.

blocks.html: List distinct roots once. If asked for multiplicities, use the polynomial factors or derivatives to determine them separately.
Counting different angle equations is not a substitute for counting distinct algebraic roots.

blocks.title: Keep the endpoint root when the cosine is one
blocks.prompt:
Solve \(4 u^{3} - 3 u - 1=0\).

Give every distinct exact real root.
blocks.hint: Recognise the multiple-angle polynomial, then choose angles so that the real roots are listed once.
blocks.solution:
Use \(u=\cos\theta\). The polynomial was obtained from \(\cos(3\theta)-1\).

Use \(0\le\theta\le\pi\).

AnglePolynomial root
\(0\)\(1\)
\(\frac{2 \pi}{3}\)\(- \frac{1}{2}\)

These values give all distinct real roots. Repeated algebraic roots give a single value in the answer set.

blocks.html: Check the degree if the equation asks for every complex root.

sections.title: How do I check that the root list is complete?
sections.label: Verify
sections.intro: For monotone fundamental ranges each admissible cosine or sine value corresponds to exactly one selected angle.

blocks.html: Check each candidate in the original polynomial. If the number of distinct values equals its degree, the root list is complete.
A numerical approximation can help you order roots but it does not establish an exact factorisation.

blocks.title: Use all distinct roots of the fifth multiple set
blocks.prompt:
Solve \(16 u^{5} - 20 u^{3} + 5 u - 1=0\).

Give the complete set of coefficients of \(\pi\) for the corresponding angles. Use \([0,\pi]\) for cosine.
blocks.hint: Recognise the multiple-angle polynomial, then choose angles so that the real roots are listed once.
blocks.solution:
Use \(u=\cos\theta\). The polynomial was obtained from \(\cos(5\theta)-1\).

Use \(0\le\theta\le\pi\).

AnglePolynomial root
\(0\)\(1\)
\(\frac{2 \pi}{5}\)\(- \frac{1}{4} + \frac{\sqrt{5}}{4}\)
\(\frac{4 \pi}{5}\)\(- \frac{\sqrt{5}}{4} - \frac{1}{4}\)

These values give all distinct real roots. Repeated algebraic roots give a single value in the answer set.

blocks.html: An optional check is to multiply the exact linear factors and compare leading coefficients.

examples.title: Read the cubic identity for cosine
examples.question: Let \(u=\cos\theta\). Express \(\cos(3\theta)\) as a polynomial in \(u\).
solution:
Take the real part of \((\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^3\).

With \(a=\cos\theta,\ b=\sin\theta\), the expansion gives \(a \left(a^{2} - 3 b^{2}\right)\).
Use \(a^2+b^2=1\) to retain just the requested variable.

examples.title: Read a fourth multiple without a sine variable
examples.question: Let \(u=\cos\theta\). Express \(\cos(4\theta)\) as a polynomial in \(u\).
solution:
Take the real part of \((\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^4\).

With \(a=\cos\theta,\ b=\sin\theta\), the expansion gives \(a^{4} - 6 a^{2} b^{2} + b^{4}\).
Use \(a^2+b^2=1\) to retain just the requested variable.

examples.title: Find the cubic identity for sine
examples.question: Let \(u=\sin\theta\). Express \(\sin(3\theta)\) as a polynomial in \(u\).
solution:
Take the imaginary part of \((\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^3\).

With \(a=\cos\theta,\ b=\sin\theta\), the expansion gives \(b \left(3 a^{2} - b^{2}\right)\).
Use \(a^2+b^2=1\) to retain just the requested variable.

examples.title: Build the full rational expression for tangent
examples.question: Let \(t=\tan\theta\). Express \(\tan 3\theta\) as a rational expression in \(t\) on the common domain.
solution:
Expand \((1+\mathrm i t)^3\) and separate its real and imaginary parts.

\(\mathrm{Re}=1 - 3 t^{2},\quad \mathrm{Im}=- t^{3} + 3 t\).
Require \(\cos\theta\ne0\) and \(\cos 3\theta\ne0\).

examples.title: Recover real roots from the triple-angle cosine
examples.question:
Solve \(4 u^{3} - 3 u=0\).

Give every distinct exact real root.
solution:
Use \(u=\cos\theta\). The polynomial was obtained from \(\cos(3\theta)-0\).

Use \(0\le\theta\le\pi\).

AnglePolynomial root
\(\frac{\pi}{6}\)\(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\)
\(\frac{\pi}{2}\)\(0\)
\(\frac{5 \pi}{6}\)\(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\)
These values give all distinct real roots. Repeated algebraic roots give a single value in the answer set.

examples.question:

Use \(0\le\theta\le\pi\).

AnglePolynomial root
\(0\)\(1\)
\(\frac{\pi}{2}\)\(0\)
\(\pi\)\(-1\)
These values give all distinct real roots. Repeated algebraic roots give a single value in the answer set.

examples.title: List all angle coefficients for the quartic identity
examples.question:
Solve \(8 u^{4} - 8 u^{2} + 1=0\).

Give the complete set of coefficients of \(\pi\) for the corresponding angles. Use \([0,\pi]\) for cosine.
solution:
Use \(u=\cos\theta\). The polynomial was obtained from \(\cos(4\theta)-0\).

Use \(0\le\theta\le\pi\).

AnglePolynomial root

extraPractice.prompt: Let \(u=\cos\theta\). Express \(\cos(2\theta)\) as a polynomial in \(u\).
extraPractice.hint: Separate the real and imaginary powers of i before replacing a square.
extraPractice.solution:
Take the real part of \((\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^2\).

With \(a=\cos\theta,\ b=\sin\theta\), the expansion gives \(a^{2} - b^{2}\).

Use \(a^2+b^2=1\) to retain just the requested variable.

extraPractice.title: Use the tangent double angle on its common domain
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(t=\tan\theta\). Express \(\tan 2\theta\) as a rational expression in \(t\) on the common domain.
extraPractice.hint: Divide both parts of \(\tfrac{\sin(n\theta)}{\cos(n\theta)}\) by \(\cos^2\theta\) on the common domain.
extraPractice.solution:
Expand \((1+\mathrm i t)^2\) and separate its real and imaginary parts.

\(\mathrm{Re}=1 - t^{2},\quad \mathrm{Im}=2 t\).

\[\tan 2\theta=\frac{2 t}{1 - t^{2}}\]

Require \(\cos\theta\ne0\) and \(\cos 2\theta\ne0\).

extraPractice.title: Find a sixth-angle identity without residual sine squares
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(u=\cos\theta\). Express \(\cos(6\theta)\) as a polynomial in \(u\).
extraPractice.hint: Separate the real and imaginary powers of i before replacing a square.
extraPractice.solution:
Take the real part of \((\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^6\).

With \(a=\cos\theta,\ b=\sin\theta\), the expansion gives \(a^{6} - 15 a^{4} b^{2} + 15 a^{2} b^{4} - b^{6}\).

Use \(a^2+b^2=1\) to retain just the requested variable.

\[\cos(6\theta)=32 u^{6} - 48 u^{4} + 18 u^{2} - 1\]

extraPractice.prompt: Let \(t=\tan\theta\). Express \(\tan 5\theta\) as a rational expression in \(t\) on the common domain. Enter the numerator and denominator separately, using a denominator with constant term 1.

\(\mathrm{Re}=5 t^{4} - 10 t^{2} + 1,\quad \mathrm{Im}=t^{5} - 10 t^{3} + 5 t\).

\[\tan 5\theta=\frac{t^{5} - 10 t^{3} + 5 t}{5 t^{4} - 10 t^{2} + 1}\]

fp2_complex_harmonics.description: Use opposite exponential powers to express sine and cosine powers as harmonics, then evaluate exact integrals.

sections.title: Why do opposite powers give real trigonometric values?
sections.label: Opposite powers
sections.intro: Set \(u=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}\). The reciprocal \(u^{-1}\) represents the angle in the opposite direction.

blocks.html: \(\cos\theta=\tfrac12(u+u^{-1})\) and \(\sin\theta=\tfrac{1}{2\mathrm i}(u-u^{-1})\) follow by adding and subtracting the exponential forms.
The difference carries a factor of \(\mathrm i\). Omitting that factor changes the value.

blocks.title: Find the constant after rewriting cosine squared
blocks.prompt: Write \(\cos^2\theta\) in harmonics of \(\theta\). Give the exact coefficient of \(1\).
blocks.hint: Pair opposite exponential powers, then simplify the factor of i and the power of 2.
blocks.solution:
Use \(u=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}\). Then \(\cos\theta=\tfrac{u+u^{-1}}2\). Keep the common denominator while expanding.

TermCoefficient
\(1\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)
\(\cos(2\theta)\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)
\[\cos^2\theta=\frac{\cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\]

blocks.html: Pair terms with the same absolute exponent.

sections.title: How do I expand a power of cosine?
sections.label: Cosine powers
sections.intro: Use the binomial theorem on the sum of opposite powers.

blocks.html: Cosine powers reduce to cosine harmonics, with a constant term for even powers. The denominator is \(2^n\).
Only zero exponent terms contribute the constant. Terms of opposite nonzero exponents give a harmonic.

blocks.title: Keep all cosine harmonics in an odd power
blocks.prompt: Write \(\cos^5\theta\) in harmonics of \(\theta\). Give the exact coefficients of \(\cos(1\theta)\), \(\cos(3\theta)\), \(\cos(5\theta)\).
blocks.hint: Pair opposite exponential powers, then simplify the factor of i and the power of 2.
blocks.solution:
Use \(u=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}\). Then \(\cos\theta=\tfrac{u+u^{-1}}2\). Keep the common denominator while expanding.

TermCoefficient
\(\cos(1\theta)\)\(\frac{5}{8}\)
\(\cos(3\theta)\)\(\frac{5}{16}\)
\(\cos(5\theta)\)\(\frac{1}{16}\)
\[\cos^5\theta=\frac{5 \cos\theta}{8} + \frac{5 \cos{\left(3 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{\cos{\left(5 \theta \right)}}{16}\]

blocks.html: Before simplifying, check the harmonics have the same parity as the original exponent.

sections.title: Why do even sine powers contain cosine harmonics?
sections.label: Even sine powers
sections.intro: An even power is unchanged when the angle changes sign.

blocks.html: Expand the difference and keep \((2\mathrm i)^n\) as a denominator until the sign is clear. Opposite powers pair into cosine terms.
The denominator can be negative for even \(n\). For fourth powers it is positive.

blocks.title: Count all harmonics with even sine parity
blocks.prompt: Write \(\sin^6\theta\) in harmonics of \(\theta\). Give the exact coefficients of \(1\), \(\cos(2\theta)\), \(\cos(4\theta)\), \(\cos(6\theta)\).
blocks.hint: Pair opposite exponential powers, then simplify the factor of i and the power of 2.
blocks.solution:
Use \(u=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}\). Then \(\sin\theta=\tfrac{u-u^{-1}}{2\mathrm i}\). Keep the common denominator while expanding.

TermCoefficient
\(1\)\(\frac{5}{16}\)
\(\cos(2\theta)\)\(- \frac{15}{32}\)
\(\cos(4\theta)\)\(\frac{3}{16}\)
\(\cos(6\theta)\)\(- \frac{1}{32}\)
\[\sin^6\theta=- \frac{15 \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{3 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{16} - \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{5}{16}\]

blocks.html: The constant term should be positive for a nonzero even power.

sections.title: Why do odd sine powers contain sine harmonics?
sections.label: Odd sine powers
sections.intro: An odd sine power changes sign with the angle, so the harmonics are also odd functions.

blocks.html: Pair equal magnitudes with opposite signs. Use \(u^k-u^{-k}=2\mathrm i\sin(k\theta)\).
The resulting trigonometric identity is real. Any remaining imaginary factor signals a simplification error.

blocks.title: Check three coefficients in the fifth sine power
blocks.prompt: Write \(\sin^5\theta\) in harmonics of \(\theta\). Give the exact coefficients of \(\sin(1\theta)\), \(\sin(3\theta)\), \(\sin(5\theta)\).
blocks.hint: Pair opposite exponential powers, then simplify the factor of i and the power of 2.
blocks.solution:
Use \(u=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}\). Then \(\sin\theta=\tfrac{u-u^{-1}}{2\mathrm i}\). Keep the common denominator while expanding.

TermCoefficient
\(\sin(1\theta)\)\(\frac{5}{8}\)
\(\sin(3\theta)\)\(- \frac{5}{16}\)
\(\sin(5\theta)\)\(\frac{1}{16}\)
\[\sin^5\theta=\frac{5 \sin\theta}{8} - \frac{5 \sin{\left(3 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{\sin{\left(5 \theta \right)}}{16}\]

blocks.html: Evaluating both sides at \(\theta=\tfrac\pi2\) quickly checks the final coefficients.

sections.title: How do harmonics make integration easier?
sections.label: Integrate
sections.intro: After expanding, integrate the constant and each sine or cosine separately.

blocks.html: \(\int\cos(k\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{\sin(k\theta)}{k}+C\) for \(k\ne0\).
The factor \(\tfrac1k\) applies to a harmonic. The constant term instead multiplies the interval length.

blocks.title: Integrate a sixth power over a half quadrant
blocks.prompt: Evaluate \(\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\sin^6\theta\,\mathrm d\theta\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Pair opposite exponential powers, then simplify the factor of i and the power of 2.
blocks.solution:
Use \(u=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}\). Then \(\sin\theta=\tfrac{u-u^{-1}}{2\mathrm i}\). Keep the common denominator while expanding.

TermCoefficient
\(1\)\(\frac{5}{16}\)
\(\cos(2\theta)\)\(- \frac{15}{32}\)
\(\cos(4\theta)\)\(\frac{3}{16}\)
\(\cos(6\theta)\)\(- \frac{1}{32}\)
\[\sin^6\theta=- \frac{15 \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{3 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{16} - \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{5}{16}\]

Integrate each harmonic. The factors from \(\int\cos(k\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta\) include \(\tfrac1k\).

blocks.html: Evaluate the antiderivative at both bounds.

sections.title: Can I predict which terms integrate to zero?
sections.label: Exact bounds
sections.intro: Look for intervals whose endpoints make entire sine or cosine terms cancel.

blocks.html: On a full period, nonconstant integer harmonics integrate to zero. On a shorter interval, evaluate each endpoint rather than assuming cancellation.
A term that vanishes at the upper endpoint may contribute through the lower endpoint.

blocks.prompt: Evaluate \(\int_{0}^{\pi}\cos^6\theta\,\mathrm d\theta\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Pair opposite exponential powers, then simplify the factor of i and the power of 2.
blocks.solution:
Use \(u=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}\). Then \(\cos\theta=\tfrac{u+u^{-1}}2\). Keep the common denominator while expanding.

TermCoefficient

blocks.html: For \(z^n=r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta}\) the circle radius is \(\sqrt[n]r\) and the roots turn by \(\tfrac{2\pi}{n}\) between neighbours.

blocks.hint: Taking moduli gives the magnitude of the parameter. Interpret the extra real-root condition, if given.
blocks.solution:
Taking moduli gives \(|k|=2^4=16\).

sections.intro: The regular set of vectors balances around the origin. Equivalently, a geometric series of the distinct unit multipliers has zero sum.

fp2_complex_sums.description: Sum finite, binomial and absolutely convergent complex series and recover the required real or imaginary part.

sections.title: What does the C + iS method combine?
sections.label: Combine components
sections.intro: Place a cosine sum in the real part and the matching sine sum in the imaginary part.

blocks.html: \(C+\mathrm iS=\sum_k a_k(\cos(k\theta)+\mathrm i\sin(k\theta))=\sum_k a_kz^k\) with unit \(z\) and real weights \(a_k\).
The method needs the same weights and angles for both component sums.

blocks.title: Give both parts of a finite sum of rotating terms
blocks.prompt:
Let \(z=1\,\mathrm e^{- \frac{i \pi}{3}}\). Consider \(\sum_{k=0}^{4} z^k\).

Give the real and imaginary parts of the sum.
blocks.hint: Check the ratio before using the formula. For an infinite sum the ratio must have modulus less than one.
blocks.solution:
Use \(\frac{z^{0}(1-z^{5})}{1-z}\).

Evaluate the powers using their moduli and arguments. The sum is \(- \frac{1}{2} - \frac{\sqrt{3} i}{2}\).

blocks.html: Take the required component only after simplifying the complex sum.

sections.title: How do I sum a finite geometric complex series?
sections.label: Finite geometric sum
sections.intro: Use the same geometric identity as for a real ratio. Complex multiplication is distributive.

blocks.html: There are \(b-a+1\) terms. The exponent in the numerator counts them.

blocks.title: Use the finite formula from a nonzero start
blocks.prompt:
Let \(z=2\,\mathrm e^{\frac{i \pi}{2}}\). Consider \(\sum_{k=1}^{5} z^k\).

Give the real and imaginary parts of the sum.
blocks.hint: Check the ratio before using the formula. For an infinite sum the ratio must have modulus less than one.
blocks.solution:
Use \(\frac{z^{1}(1-z^{5})}{1-z}\).

Evaluate the powers using their moduli and arguments. The sum is \(12 + 26 i\).

blocks.html: Check the starting index before using the formula.

sections.title: What if the ratio is exactly one?
sections.label: Exceptional ratio
sections.intro: At ratio one each power equals one. The expression with denominator \(1-z\) is undefined.

blocks.html: Count the terms directly when \(z=1\).
If \(|z|=1\) but \(z\ne1\), the finite formula is still valid.

blocks.title: Handle the ratio-one case without dividing
blocks.prompt:
Let \(z=1\). Consider \(\sum_{k=1}^{5} z^k\).

Find the exact real part of the sum.
blocks.hint: Check the ratio before using the formula. For an infinite sum the ratio must have modulus less than one.
blocks.solution:
Here \(z=1\), so every term is 1. There are \(5\) terms.

Evaluate the powers using their moduli and arguments. The sum is \(5\).

blocks.html: The infinite sum is a separate convergence question.

sections.title: When can a complex geometric series converge?
sections.label: Convergence
sections.intro: The powers tend to zero if and only if the ratio has modulus less than one, for a geometric series with nonzero first term.

blocks.html: \(\sum_{k=a}^{\infty}z^k=\frac{z^a}{1-z}\) for \(|z|<1\). The series then converges absolutely.
A negative real part does not guarantee convergence. Check the full modulus.

blocks.title: Recover the imaginary part of a convergent sum
blocks.prompt:
Let \(z=\frac{1}{3}\,\mathrm e^{\frac{i \pi}{2}}\). Consider \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty z^k\).

Find the exact imaginary part of the sum.
blocks.hint: Check the ratio before using the formula. For an infinite sum the ratio must have modulus less than one.
blocks.solution:
The series converges absolutely because \(|z|=\frac{1}{3}<1\). Use \(\frac{z^{0}}{1-z}\).

Evaluate the powers using their moduli and arguments. The sum is \(\frac{9}{10} + \frac{3 i}{10}\).

blocks.html: At modulus one the terms do not tend to zero.

sections.title: How do binomial coefficients change the method?
sections.label: Binomial sums
sections.intro: If the weights are binomial coefficients, use the binomial expansion of a sum instead of the geometric formula.

blocks.html: \(\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk a^{n-k}z^k=(a+z)^n\).
Take care of any factor multiplying each power. It may belong in the choice of ratio or in the binomial base.

blocks.title: Use the binomial weights for a sine sum
blocks.prompt:
Let \(z=2\,\mathrm e^{\frac{i \pi}{2}}\).

Evaluate \(\sum_{k=0}^{4}\binom{4}{k}\left(2\right)^k\sin\left(k\cdot \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Combine the real and imaginary sums as one complex binomial sum, then deal with the starting index.
blocks.solution:
The binomial theorem gives the sum from 0 as \((1+z)^{4}\).

The complex total is \(-7 - 24 i\). Take the requested component or give both.

blocks.html: Use de Moivre to evaluate a high power when it has a convenient argument.

sections.title: What if one or more starting terms are missing?
sections.label: Shifted index
sections.intro: Compute the full geometric or binomial expression only if you can remove the unwanted terms.

blocks.html: Subtract the omitted contribution before taking its real or imaginary part.
The first omitted binomial term is \(a^n\). It affects the real sum even when its imaginary contribution is zero.

blocks.title: Remove two terms from a real component
blocks.prompt:
Let \(z=1\,\mathrm e^{\frac{i \pi}{2}}\).

Evaluate \(\sum_{k=2}^{5}\binom{5}{k}2^{5-k}\left(1\right)^k\cos\left(k\cdot \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Combine the real and imaginary sums as one complex binomial sum, then deal with the starting index.
blocks.solution:
The binomial theorem gives the sum from 0 as \((2+z)^{5}\).

Remove the 2 initial terms, because the requested sum starts at 2.

The complex total is \(-70 - 39 i\). Take the requested component or give both.

blocks.html: For weighted trigonometric sums, check the powers, trigonometric frequency and the starting index.

solution: Here \(z=1\), so every term is 1. There are \(5\) terms.
Evaluate the powers using their moduli and arguments. The sum is \(5\).

examples.question:

Give the real and imaginary parts of the sum.
solution: The series converges absolutely because \(|z|=\frac{1}{2}<1\). Use \(\frac{z^{2}}{1-z}\).
Evaluate the powers using their moduli and arguments. The sum is \(- \frac{1}{5} - \frac{i}{10}\).

examples.question:

Evaluate \(\sum_{k=0}^{4}\binom{4}{k}z^k\). Give the real and imaginary parts.
solution: The binomial theorem gives the sum from 0 as \((1+z)^{4}\).
The complex total is \(-4\). Take the requested component or give both.

examples.question:
Let \(z=1\,\mathrm e^{\frac{i \pi}{3}}\).

Evaluate \(\sum_{k=2}^{5}\binom{5}{k}\left(1\right)^k\cos\left(k\cdot \frac{\pi}{3}\right)\) exactly.
solution: The binomial theorem gives the sum from 0 as \((1+z)^{5}\).
Remove the 2 initial terms, because the requested sum starts at 2.
The complex total is \(-17 + 2 \sqrt{3} i\). Take the requested component or give both.

extraPractice.title: Take the real part after two omitted powers
extraPractice.prompt:
Let \(z=1\,\mathrm e^{\frac{i \pi}{4}}\). Consider \(\sum_{k=2}^{6} z^k\).

Find the exact real part of the sum.
extraPractice.hint: Check the ratio before using the formula. For an infinite sum the ratio must have modulus less than one.
extraPractice.solution:
Use \(\frac{z^{2}(1-z^{5})}{1-z}\).

Evaluate the powers using their moduli and arguments. The sum is \(- \sqrt{2} - 1\).
